content:
Hi everyone, I want to share a 6-file Lean 4 project formalizing a proof of Seymour's Second Neighborhood Conjecture, which is now live on my GitHub: github.com

The conjecture asks if every oriented graph (a directed graph without bidirectional edges or loops) consists of a node whose second neighborhood is at least as large as its first N^2(v) \geq N^1(v). I have been wrestling with this problem for quite some time. The lake build passes cleanly through five files, though the complete proof is in file 5.

Each lake file looks at a different stage of (my approach) to the proof. Initially I set up the oriented graph because (to my knowledge) Lean does not have oriented graphs. Then I build a custom data structure based on my own definitions. This is because standard graph theory terminology is not suitable for this problem, allowing in particular for Seymour diamonds. Files 2 - 5 are different branches of the flow chart that need to be exhausted to rid ourselves of back arcs.

The repository matches the framework of my arXiv preprint (“A Minimum Counterexample Proof of the Seymour Second Neighborhood Conjecture via the Graph Level Order”). I have been doing this because some of the advice I have been receiving lately (both online and in person) since I announced that I had a solution to the conjecture was to code it up in Lean.

What I am working on right now: I am currently updating Version 15 of the arXiv paper. While the current public version on the main arxiv page is v14, v15 will be focused on providing (1) ensuring that there are no gaps in the proofs as there were in v14 (2) ensuring that the claims do not overclaim their results, and (3) providing normal English explanations of the exact steps taken in the Lean code.

My approach: The core of the proof uses a custom BFS coordinate system (the Graph Level Order) to show that a Minimum Counterexample must be total-degree regular. One other update between v14 and v15 is how I changed my definition of an MCE. I noticed that "tail graphs" could still be MCEs in v14's definition. So in the LEAN code, I updated the definition to be a multi-variable MCE that excluded those graphs.

This forces a distance-based equivalence relation where the neighborhood density collapses symmetrically via the binomial theorem in File 5.

What I'm asking for: I would be deeply grateful for any eyes on the repository—especially the base graph definitions in File 0—to ensure no subtle edge cases or hidden assumptions slipped through the type system before the final v15 release. I have embedded flowcharts and sketches in the repo to show the spatial intuition behind the code!

I come from a background in programming, but it is in C++/Java/JavaScript/Python. This journey to functional programming has not been a cakewalk.

The Importance of my approach: The Conjecture generally seeks for a single node whose second neighborhood is at least as large as its first. My framework establishes a strengthening of the SSNC. By defining the Minimum Counterexample (MCE) using a lexicographic minimization of the total number of interior arcs and the maximum total interior degree, the graph is choked into absolute total-degree uniformity. If I am correct, this equivalence relation will make the entire last rooted neighborhood consist of all Seymour vertices.

As a result, the final neighborhood layer partitions into a distance-based equivalence relation. The final proof in File 5 doesn't just isolate one vertex; it uses the binomial theorem to prove a global collapse where an entire neighborhood layer of vertices collectively satisfies the Seymour inequality.

The directory also contains images that help explain the overall data structure, for charts explaining the proof, the tail graph and why it wouldn't last under the new MCE (if my lean is right), and how the algorithm performed with different test minimum degree nodes.
